claims.text: The initial material is a W–Cu metal-matrix composite without graphene reinforcement.
The proposed intervention is the addition of 1–5 vol% graphene to the W–Cu composite.
Introducing graphene during processing will form graphene bridges between the tungsten and copper phases.
The graphene reinforcement will be located at tungsten–copper interfaces.
Graphene has high in-plane thermal conductivity.
Interfacial graphene will act as an efficient thermal bridge across W–Cu phase boundaries.
Graphene thermal bridges will facilitate heat transfer through the composite.
Adding controlled graphene reinforcement will increase the thermal conductivity of W–Cu relative to an otherwise comparable graphene-free composite.
The graphene-reinforced composite will retain mechanical durability comparable to that of the graphene-free W–Cu baseline.
The graphene-reinforced composite will retain resistance to irradiation-induced damage comparable to that of the graphene-free W–Cu baseline.
Graphene reinforcement will not compromise mechanical interlocking in the W–Cu matrix.
Graphene reinforcement will not compromise the irradiation tolerance of the W–Cu matrix.
The predicted effect should hold in high-temperature and neutron-irradiation environments representative of heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications.
The predicted effect depends on graphene being uniformly dispersed and optimized within the proposed 1–5 vol% range.
Excessive graphene concentration or poor dispersion may reduce mechanical durability or create processing defects.
Processing variations and graphene dispersion quality may affect the final thermal, mechanical, and irradiation-related properties.
